Why does reviewing every line of agent output defeat the point of using agents?
column2: It caps the whole system at human reading speed. Replace most reading with automated checks and spot checks. [I01 · Get the human out of the code loop]

column1: If the human stops reading the code, what replaces line-by-line review?
column2: Deterministic evidence: CRAP scores, mutation testing, acceptance/QA scripts, plus occasional spot checks. [I01 · Get the human out of the code loop]

column1: Is code quality irrelevant when agents write the code? Why or why not?
column2: No. Mess compounds for agents too; past some level they thrash and stop making progress. Clean code is an input to agent productivity. [I02 · Mess compounds, for agents too]

column1: Define the productivity margin.
column2: Human time for a task divided by agents-plus-gates time. It must stay above 1. [I03 · The productivity margin is the scoreboard]

column1: What margin does Uncle Bob report with his full gate stack, and how strong is that evidence?
column2: Roughly 2x-5x (about an hour for his full pipeline vs about half a day for a human). It's his personal experience, not a controlled study. [I03 · The productivity margin is the scoreboard]

column1: What is the 'lost in the middle' effect?
column2: LLMs use information at the beginning and end of a long context better than information in the middle (a U-shaped curve; Liu et al., TACL 2024). [I04 · Steering decays]

column1: What does Uncle Bob do about long instruction files?
column2: Trims the initial prompt to the absolute minimum so it all sits in the high-attention zone, then enforces everything else with deterministic tools afterward. [I04 · Steering decays]

column1: What's the difference between a rule and a gate?
column2: A rule is prompt text the model may weight weakly. A gate is a deterministic pass/fail tool the agent must satisfy before it can finish. [I05 · The deterministic-tool loop]

column1: Why do gates compose better than prompt rules?
column2: Adding a gate doesn't weaken the others. Adding a prompt rule competes for attention and dilutes the rest. [I05 · The deterministic-tool loop]

column1: How should the length of agent-facing and human-facing documents differ?
column2: Agent-facing documents can be long (front-load what matters) because agents read them. Human-facing summaries must be short because humans don't read agent output. [I06 · The reading asymmetry]

column1: Write the CRAP formula.
column2: CRAP = CC^2 x (1 - coverage)^3 + CC, where CC is cyclomatic complexity and coverage is a fraction from 0 to 1. [I07 · The CRAP metric as a gate]

column1: What is the CRAP score of a fully tested function with CC = 6?
column2: Exactly 6. At 100% coverage CRAP equals CC. [I07 · The CRAP metric as a gate]
column3: uncle-bob-ai ch03 I07 gates metrics testing

column1: CC = 3, no tests. CRAP score? Does it pass a threshold of 6?
column2: 9 + 3 = 12. It fails. [I07 · The CRAP metric as a gate]
column3: uncle-bob-ai ch03 I07 gates metrics testing

column1: CC = 7 and 100% coverage. Can it pass a threshold of 6?
column2: No. CRAP = 7 > 6, so you must reduce complexity (split the function). [I07 · The CRAP metric as a gate]

column1: What does it mean when a mutant 'survives'?
column2: The code was changed and every test still passed, so no assertion pins down that behavior. [I08 · Mutation testing as the merciless hardener]

column1: Your tests have 100% line coverage, yet a mutant survives. What does that tell you?
column2: The line ran, but nothing checked its exact behavior. Coverage measures execution; mutation testing measures detection. [I08 · Mutation testing as the merciless hardener]

column1: Why is a literal 100% mutation score usually unreachable?
column2: Equivalent mutants: changes that don't alter behavior and so can't be killed. Excuse them with a written reason. [I08 · Mutation testing as the merciless hardener]

column1: What selection rule does the episode suggest for reviving old techniques?
column2: Look for ideas that were sound but shelved only because they were too tedious or slow for humans. Agents remove that cost. [I09 · Agents don't feel boredom]

column1: Name the five seats of the relay in order.
column2: Specifier, Coder, Cleaner, Hardener, QA. [I10 · The five-seat relay]

column1: What does the specifier produce?
column2: A Gherkin (given/when/then) acceptance test and a QA procedure written from the point of view of a human using the system through its UI. [I10 · The five-seat relay]

column1: Which seat runs CRAP and which runs mutation testing?
column2: The cleaner runs CRAP analysis and code review; the hardener runs mutation testing. [I10 · The five-seat relay]

column1: What are the benefit and the cost of single-task, fresh-context agents?
column2: Benefit: small focused contexts (less lost-in-the-middle) and parallelism. Cost: startup time (around 10-15 s) and rebuilding understanding of the codebase each time. [I11 · Born, do the task, die]

column1: An agent session drifted into a bad approach. Keep correcting it, or restart?
column2: Usually restart with better instructions. A session's trajectory persists, and only clearing the context clears it. [I12 · A context window has momentum]

column1: In Uncle Bob's workflow, who designs the module structure?
column2: The human. He interrogates agents about the existing structure, designs the target himself, and hands over an implementation plan. [I13 · Interrogate the agents about structure]

column1: What instrument did Uncle Bob have his agents build to supervise structure?
column2: An architecture viewer: a clickable UML-style diagram of modules, dependency directions, submodules and code. [I14 · Agents build your instruments]

column1: Name the three standard repairs when the dependency fence fails.
column2: Invert the dependency, insert an interface, or split the module. [I15 · The dependency fence]

column1: Why should agents not be allowed to edit the fence file to make the gate pass?
column2: Changing allowed dependencies is a design decision that belongs to the human. Otherwise the gate means nothing. [I15 · The dependency fence]

column1: Why does module partitioning help agents?
column2: Models compartmentalize like humans (they're modeled after us). Focused modules keep the relevant context small and unpolluted. [I16 · Compartmentalization serves models too]

column1: What is a deep module and why do agents benefit?
column2: A module with a small, simple interface hiding a large implementation. Agents can use it from the interface and tests without spending context on internals. [I17 · Deep modules are context economy]

column1: What danger did Uncle Bob flag about agents relying on interfaces?
column2: They may not read the code beneath. That's fine only if the implementation is consistent with the interface. [I17 · Deep modules are context economy]

column1: Using TDD, explain 'values, not disciplines'.
column2: Value: every behavior is tested. Discipline: the red-green-refactor micro-cycle. Agents get the value (enforced by gates) but not the ritual. [I18 · Values transfer, disciplines don't, thresholds move]

column1: What CRAP thresholds does Uncle Bob use for humans vs agents?
column2: Below about 4 for humans; 6 for agents, considering 8. [I18 · Values transfer, disciplines don't, thresholds move]
column3: uncle-bob-ai ch06 I18 values testing metrics

column1: Why does he loosen the threshold for agents, and is that established?
column2: He says agents have a huge, accurate short-term memory. It's his hypothesis, not independently verified. [I18 · Values transfer, disciplines don't, thresholds move]
column3: uncle-bob-ai ch06 I18 values testing metrics

column1: An agent argues convincingly that your threshold should be 8. What do you do?
column2: Treat it as a hypothesis: try 8 and measure thrash, defects and margin. An agent debate is not evidence. [I19 · Agent debates are hypothesis generators]

column1: Why does Uncle Bob compare heavy agent specs to waterfall?
column2: Both assume you can specify everything up front. Agents hit unanticipated cases, go off course, and you have to back up and re-plan. [I20 · Heavy up-front specs are waterfall replayed]

column1: How often does Uncle Bob step in to look at architecture?
column2: After every story or two, then he lets the agents continue. [I21 · Agile small batches for agents]

column1: State the $1-house argument in one sentence.
column2: When change is nearly free, expensive up-front design (which exists to avoid costly change) stops paying for itself, so you iterate. [I22 · The one-dollar house]

column1: Where does the $1-house argument NOT apply well?
column2: Wherever change is still expensive: data migrations, public APIs, hardware, regulated systems, external users. [I22 · The one-dollar house]

column1: Do Uncle Bob's specs persist? What serves as the specification?
column2: No, they're ephemeral. The working end result serves as the specification. [I23 · Specs are ephemeral; the result is the spec]

column1: Uncle Bob published his CRAP tool, mutation tester and harness. What does he say to do with them?
column2: Don't download them. Point your agents at them, let them study the tools, and have them build your own customized versions. [I24 · Point, don't download]

column1: Tactical vs strategic programming: which do agents do well?
column2: Tactical (getting this change working). Strategic design investment remains the human's job. [I25 · Agents are sergeants, humans are generals]

column1: Describe the 'human as subagent' stage.
column2: A junior receives the same tasks agents get and goes through the same deterministic gates under a lead, for months, before being trusted to run agents. [I26 · Human as subagent: the education gauntlet]

column1: What is the learning ladder Uncle Bob describes?
column2: Binary, assembly, a language like C, a higher-level language like Python, then strategically running an agent under supervision. [I26 · Human as subagent: the education gauntlet]

column1: Why can an experienced engineer spot agent thrash that a novice misses?
column2: They've been through the same struggle, so they recognize looping, fix-one-break-another and spinning. [I27 · Recognizing thrash is the key skill]

column1: Which 'old books' does Uncle Bob recommend?
column2: Works by Tom DeMarco and Ed Yourdon, and The Pragmatic Programmer, filtering out what's dated. [I27 · Recognizing thrash is the key skill]

column1: Why do software fundamentals still matter when models write the code?
column2: They organize complexity into understandable pieces, and models benefit from the same organization as humans. Discarded rules tend to come back. [I28 · Fundamentals persist up every abstraction rung]
